pages.x: Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, put back on his throne in 1953 by a coup backed by the United States and Britain, used Iran's oil money to build a modern state and army. But his secret police jailed and tortured opponents, and many Iranians felt their country was run for the rich and for foreigners.

From exile in Iraq and then France, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, a senior Shia cleric, attacked the shah as a puppet of America. His sermons were smuggled into Iran on cassette tapes and copied by the thousand. Through 1978 the protests grew, and soldiers fired on crowds again and again.

Strikes shut down the oil fields, and millions marched in Tehran. On 16 January 1979 the shah flew out of Iran, never to return. On 1 February Khomeini landed in Tehran to a welcome by millions. Within days the army gave up, and in a vote that spring Iranians chose an Islamic Republic.

In November 1979 students loyal to Khomeini stormed the American embassy in Tehran and took 52 Americans hostage. They were held for 444 days, and a rescue mission ended in disaster in a desert sandstorm. The crisis broke relations between Iran and the United States, which have never been restored.

The new state was ruled by clerics, with Khomeini as Supreme Leader. Women had to cover their hair, and many of the liberals and leftists who had joined the revolution were jailed or executed. In 1980 Iraq invaded, beginning an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands.

The revolution created the first modern state ruled by Islamic clerics and inspired Islamist movements across the Muslim world. It made Iran and the United States bitter enemies. Inside Iran, protests against its strict rules, like those led by women in 2022, still challenge the system it built.
